intro: Lazur is an AI assistant for literary agents who work on a Mac. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on your screen, and Lazur answers out loud. It works in Gmail, Outlook, Word and Chrome, and it is not a plugin for any of them.
tldr: Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. You hold a key, ask a question, and it answers out loud while pointing at the screen.
Agents lose much of the day to email, editor calls and reading after dark. Lazur helps with questions, short drafts and finding the right control.
Lazur does not click buttons or act in your apps. It points, guides one click at a time, drafts text and types what you dictate.
Client manuscripts and contracts are confidential. Check your agency's rules before any AI tool sees them.
Start with one job, such as editor replies or Track Changes in Word, and keep the habit only if it saves you real time.

blocks.text: A literary agent's computer day is mostly email, with long stretches of reading tucked around it. You answer editors, chase responses, read queries and proposals, and edit client work in Word. An AI assistant for literary agents helps most where the day gets lost: finding the right button, sorting a thread, drafting a short reply and writing a quick note. Lazur works that way on the Mac.
Where a literary agent's day goes
No survey I could open measures how literary agents spend their computer time. The evidence below is indirect, so read it as a pattern, not a benchmark.

Nathan Bransford, a literary agent, kept a day diary in 2008. It lists about 6 hours 25 minutes of answering email across three blocks. That total is an upper bound, because the morning block from 8:00 to 11:45 also covered calls to editors. The same diary shows a 1 hour 45 minute lunch with an editor, and one hour spent writing comments on a client proposal. Manuscript reading began at 6:15 pm.

Broader numbers point the same way. Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index says the average worker gets 117 emails a day, and most are skimmed in under 60 seconds. The same report says 29% of active workers return to their inboxes by 10 pm. That survey covers general knowledge workers using Microsoft 365, not literary agents, so use it as context.
Email triage: the biggest block of your day

Email is where most agents start the day and where many get stuck. Booher Research says an agent often gets 50 to 100 email pitches a day. That is an informal estimate, not a measured count. Even at the low end, each message needs a decision: pass, request, or hand it to a reader.

Triage works best in three passes. First, sort by sender: editors, clients and queries. Second, flag what needs an answer today. Third, handle the rest in one block, not in ten small gaps. Lazur helps most in the first pass, when you need to know what a message actually asks.

Here is a worked example. An editor sends a long thread about a proposal you pitched a few weeks ago. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask, 'What does this editor want from me?' Lazur reads the thread on screen and answers out loud. You then decide whether the reply can wait for the afternoon block, or whether it needs a note today.
Three habits make triage faster. Each one works with the inbox you already have.

items: Put the stage in the subject line, such as 'Query: full request' or 'Contract: revisions'.
Make a Gmail label for each stage, then filter on it. Ask Lazur to walk you through it with the steps at /how-to/create-a-label-in-gmail.
Snooze threads that wait on someone else. The steps are at /how-to/snooze-an-email-in-gmail.
Schedule nudges to editors for mid-morning instead of early morning. See /how-to/schedule-an-email-to-send-later-in-gmail.

blocks.text: The common mistake is answering every message as it lands. That keeps you in the inbox all day. Batch your replies into one or two windows, then close the window and read in peace.
Reading queries and proposals after hours

Booher Research says agents often read proposals on weekends or late in the evening. Daytime goes to pitching, selling, negotiating contracts and networking with editors. Two or three readers often screen proposals before the agent reads them. If you are one of those readers, the reading lands on your evenings.

Lazur does not judge a book for you. It can read a page on screen aloud, explain what a passage does, or say what a sample chapter covers. That saves setup time. It does not replace your taste, and it should not replace the first page you read yourself.

Here is a worked example. A query arrives late in the evening with a pasted synopsis and three sample pages. Open the sample in Word or Gmail. Ask Lazur, 'Summarize the first page in three sentences.' Lazur answers out loud. Then read the first page yourself before you decide what to request.

Before you request a full manuscript, check the word count, the genre fit, the comparison titles and the sample. Lazur can point you to each item in the submission email, one at a time. Do not let it make the call. The request is your judgment, and your name goes on it.

The mistake to avoid is letting a summary stand in for the sample. A summary misses voice, pacing and the sentence that makes you keep reading. Use summaries to find your place in a long file, then read the pages that matter.
Editor calls, outreach and the admin around them

Bransford's diary puts calls and lunches in the middle of the day. The admin around them takes the rest: notes after a call, follow-ups, contract questions and revised deal memos. Each task is small. Together they fill the afternoon.

Dictation fits this work. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Dictation includes snippets, a personal dictionary and clipboard slots. Add your clients' names and imprint names to the personal dictionary before a busy week, so they come out right the first time.

Here is a worked example. Right after a call, hold fn and say: Call with the editor. Wants a revised synopsis by Friday. Asked about audio rights, follow up Monday. The note lands at the cursor. Check the wording, then paste it into the client file.
Write the note within the hour. Notes fade fast after three or four calls in a row. If you need a place to park the note, ask Lazur to open Apple Notes and point at the new note button.
Editing client work in Word on Mac

Client work in Word is slow because every comment needs context. Track Changes and comments keep edits visible, so the author can see what changed and why. In Word for Mac, Track Changes lives under Review > Track Changes, and the shortcut is ⌘ ⇧ E.

Ask Lazur where a control is when you cannot find it. Lazur circles the button and puts a label on it. It does not press the button for you. You click, then you keep working. That rule keeps you in control of the file.

Here is a worked example. A client sends back a proposal with dozens of comments inside. Ask Lazur, 'Where do I add a comment?' Lazur points at the Review tab and labels the comment button. You write each comment yourself. For the full steps, see /how-to/add-a-comment-in-word.

blocks.title: Save a clean copy first
blocks.text: Save a clean copy of the client file before a new round of edits. Track Changes is easy to switch off by accident, and a clean copy gives you a fallback.

The mistake to watch for is leaving Track Changes on across the whole file without checking. Look at the status before you send. Clients notice when a file shows every stray keystroke. For Word formats and templates, see /for/literary-agents/word.
How an AI assistant for literary agents works on your Mac

Lazur lives in the notch at the top of your screen. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where something is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.

Hold fn to dictate. Lazur also handles everyday tasks by voice: timers, Apple Reminders, Calendar events, notes, music and volume, opening apps and links, web search and Shortcuts. Research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs through the Lazur for Chrome extension, then comes back with a summary and a report.

Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. It is not a plugin or add-in for any app, and it has no partnership with any app maker. Think of it as a colleague beside your work, not a hand inside it.

blocks.title: Read every draft first
blocks.text: Lazur drafts text and types it where you ask. Nothing leaves your outbox until you send it. Read every draft to an editor or client before it goes out.
A realistic day with Lazur

The day in this section is plausible, not a record of a real agent. It follows the pattern in Bransford's diary: email early, calls in the middle, admin in the afternoon and reading at night. Your times will differ. The asks stay short, because that is how you talk to Lazur mid-task.
Notice the pattern. Most asks are a single question, a single draft or a single reminder. Lazur helps with the piece you are stuck on, then you return to the work.

If you run Apple Mail, its guide covers searching email. It does not cover rules or Smart Mailboxes, so test those on a sample folder before you rely on them for submissions.

Many agents keep a submissions spreadsheet next to the inbox. For formulas and sorting in Google Sheets, see /apps/google-sheets. If your inbox runs in Gmail through Chrome, the agent guide covers queries, templates and filters at /for/literary-agents/gmail.
Privacy, client confidentiality and your agency's rules

Manuscripts, unsold proposals and contracts are confidential. Your authors trust you with them. Before any AI tool sees that material, check your agency's policy and your author agreements. Do not assume a tool is allowed because it runs on your Mac.

Here is how Lazur handles data, as this site describes it. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is not used to train AI models. Memory of what you asked and did stays on the Mac.

blocks.title: Not a compliance claim
blocks.text: This page describes Lazur's data handling. It does not describe a compliance certification, and it is not legal advice. Ask your agency before you use Lazur on client material.
A practical rule: use Lazur on your own drafts, your own emails and public text first. Ask your agency before you use it on an unsold manuscript or a signed contract.
Mistakes agents make with AI tools

items: Trusting a summary in place of the sample. Read the first page yourself before a request goes out.
Sending a draft without reading it. Lazur drafts text, but you own every word an editor reads.
Expecting Lazur to act in your apps. It points, guides, answers and types. You click and send.
Starting with the hardest job. Start with triage or Word comments, where a small gain adds up fastest.
Dictating names wrong. Fix the personal dictionary before a week of calls.

blocks.text: Setting up Lazur for your agency work

items: Download Lazur from /download and open it on your Mac. It runs on Apple silicon and Intel Macs.
Start with the email you are answering now. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask what it wants.
Add editor names and imprint names to the personal dictionary before you dictate.
Make a Gmail label for the query stage. Follow /how-to/create-a-label-in-gmail with Lazur guiding you.
Try one Word job on a copy of a client file, such as Track Changes.
Check the trial and plan terms on /pricing before you decide.

blocks.text: What to do next

Pick one job for the next few working days. Choose triage, one Word round or query reading. Time the task before and after you use Lazur. Keep the habit if it saves you real minutes, and drop it if it does not.

faq.question: Is Lazur built only for literary agents?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that works in any app. This page shows how a literary agent can use it for email, reading and Word work. It is not a separate agent edition.

faq.question: Does Lazur read my inbox in the background?
faq.answer: No. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Memory of your requests stays on the Mac.

faq.question: Can Lazur send emails or submit queries for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur drafts and types text where you ask, and it points at things. It does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. You read the draft and press send.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Windows is planned, not available. Lazur runs on macOS, on both Apple silicon and Intel Macs.

faq.question: Which version of Outlook for Mac should I run?
faq.answer: Microsoft's release notes list Outlook for Mac 16.114.3, build 26102720, released October 27, 2026. Updates need macOS 14 or later. The App Store listing shows 16.114.4, so check the build your copy shows.

faq.question: Can I use Lazur on confidential manuscripts or contracts?
faq.answer: Follow your agency's rules and your author agreements first. This site does not claim any compliance certification. Ask your agency before you use Lazur on unsold manuscripts or signed contracts.

faq.question: Is there a way to try Lazur before I pay?
faq.answer: Lazur offers a free trial that needs no credit card. Check /pricing for the current terms, since plans can change.

faq.question: Is QueryManager free for literary agents?
faq.answer: QueryManager's FAQ says it is free for agents, publishers and authors. It is web-based and needs a modern browser. The FAQ does not mention a Mac app, so use it in Chrome or Safari.

faq.question: How do I find a button I cannot see in Word?
faq.answer: Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask where the button is. Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Then you click it yourself. For Word basics, see /for/literary-agents/word.

painPoints.title: Email never really stops
painPoints.text: Microsoft's 2025 survey puts the average worker at 117 emails a day. Booher Research says agents often get 50 to 100 pitches a day, an informal estimate.

painPoints.title: Reading lands after dark
painPoints.text: Agents often read proposals on weekends or late in the evening, because daytime goes to pitching, contracts and editor networking.

painPoints.title: Calls take the middle of the day
painPoints.text: Bransford's 2008 diary shows morning calls to editors and a 1 hour 45 minute lunch with an editor cutting into email and writing time.

painPoints.title: Client edits take long afternoons
painPoints.text: Writing comments on one client proposal took one hour in Bransford's diary. A full client list multiplies that time across the week.

painPoints.title: Interruptions every two minutes
painPoints.text: Microsoft reports that employees are interrupted every 2 minutes by a meeting, an email or a notification. Agents face the same pattern in their inboxes.

painPoints.title: Tools that do not fit the Mac
painPoints.text: QueryManager is web-based and its FAQ lists no Mac app. Apple's Mail guide is written for macOS 27 and skips rules and Smart Mailboxes.
